rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Usury” is a common rendering of ribā, but the terms are not synonymous: not all interest is ribā, and not all ribā is interest.
rows.anchor: Usury is the usual translation for ribā, and this commentary follows this common rendering. However, it must be noted that these terms are not strictly synonymous.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ribā means increase, gain, or growth and covers deferment and surplus transactions; it is a complex area of Islamic law.
rows.anchor: Ribā simply means “increase,” “gain,” or “growth,” and in the Quran and Ḥadīth it refers to two main types of transactions:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pre-Islamic deferment ribā charged a fee when an interest-free loan came due.
rows.anchor: In pre-Islamic Arabia the ribā of deferment was the charging of a fee on an interest-free loan once it came due.

rows.speaker: Imām Mālik
rows.claim: Mālik describes a creditor demanding payment or an increase at maturity, then increasing the debt and extending its term if payment was not made.
rows.anchor: The founder of the Mālikī school of law, Imām Mālik

rows.speaker: Many
rows.claim: Many understand the Quran’s permission of trade and prohibition of ribā as targeting deferment added to existing loans at maturity.
rows.anchor: Many believe that the general prohibitions in the Quran allowing trade but forbidding ribā refer to this practice, which was a deferment on already existing loans at the time of their maturity.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeated doubling could multiply a debt radically within a year and eventually strip a debtor of all possessions; 3:130 names this compounding.
rows.anchor: This radical compounding is mentioned in 3:130: O you who believe! Devour not usury, doubling and multiplying

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited hadith requires six named commodities to be exchanged in equal amounts, hand to hand, and says any increase is ribā.
rows.anchor: there is a ḥadīth that says, “Gold for gold, silver for silver, wheat for wheat, barley for barley, dates for dates, and salt for salt;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Surplus ribā is the disparity in quantities between traded objects.
rows.anchor: the disparity in amounts between the two objects traded.

rows.speaker: Bilāl
rows.claim: Bilāl brought the Prophet high-quality dates and explained that he had exchanged two measures of lower-quality dates for one measure of them.
rows.anchor: the Companion Bilāl visited the Prophet with some high-quality dates, and the Prophet inquired about their source. Bilāl explained that he traded two volumes of lower-quality dates for one volume

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet calls Bilāl’s unequal date exchange forbidden ribā and instructs him to sell the first dates, then use the proceeds to buy the better ones.
rows.anchor: The Prophet said, “This is precisely the forbidden ribā! Do not do this. Instead, sell the first type of dates, and use the proceeds to buy the other.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even equal same-kind trades are barred across time because delayed use makes present and future amounts unequal; this surplus logic applies to trade, not charitable loans.
rows.anchor: the stipulation “like for like, hand to hand, in equal amounts” was understood to prevent trading, for example, an ounce of gold now for an ounce of gold at some point in the future.

rows.speaker: jurists
rows.claim: Jurists disagree whether the relevant attribute of the six commodities is measurability, fungibility, storability, use as food, or a combination.
rows.anchor: jurists disagreed over whether the relevant legal attribute of these six commodities in the aforementioned ḥadīth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jurists extend ribā rules to other items according to whether those items possess the legally relevant attributes.
rows.anchor: Based upon this reasoning, they would then extend the ribā rules to other items based upon whether they possessed the relevant attributes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two ribā prohibitions concern different transactions—credit cost and same-kind commodity trades—yet share a name and raise a common moral question.
rows.anchor: jurists have tried to understand the moral question underlying two seemingly quite different kinds of transactions, one involving the cost of credit, the other involving trade

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some understand both prohibitions as protecting against unfair pricing.
rows.anchor: Some have seen, in both types of ribā prohibitions, a protection against unfair pricing.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For goods of the same kind but differing quality or time, the Prophet’s resale method anchors the exchange in fairly priced market conditions; credit prices can be negotiated fairly.
rows.anchor: thus grounding the sale in fairly priced existing market conditions.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gharar means unlawful transaction risk, and its Arabic semantic link to ghurūr connects risk with deception.
rows.anchor: The rules about ribā, moreover, are always understood in terms of risk, which in Arabic is called gharar, a word semantically linked to “deception”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlawful uncertainty can make a sale equivalent to gambling; a cited hadith forbids sales of unknown, unmeasured, undistributed, or undetermined goods and catches.
rows.anchor: Thus in a ḥadīth it is said, “The Prophet has forbidden the purchase of the unborn animal in its mother’s womb, the sale of the milk in the udder without measurement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One cannot sell something one does not possess, whose attributes are unknown, or that does not yet exist.
rows.anchor: Thus one cannot sell an item one does not actually possess, whose attributes are unknown, or that does not yet exist.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because some risk exists in all honest trade, jurists permit certain forward sales of nonexistent agricultural goods for social and economic benefit and sometimes necessity.
rows.anchor: Since risk is always present in some form in all honest business transactions, jurists allowed certain kinds of transactions, such as forward sales on agricultural products

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forward crop sales were practiced in Madinah, but the Prophet and later jurists imposed strict conditions to limit excessive risk and prevent ribā cover.
rows.anchor: Forward sales of crops were practiced in Madinah (see v. 282), though the Prophet set strict conditions on them

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some say this ribā passage was among the last revelations, perhaps the last.
rows.anchor: It is said by some that this passage dealing with ribā was one of the last or even the last to be revealed;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other verses sometimes called the final revelation are 4:176 and 5:3.
rows.anchor: 4:176 and 5:3 are also sometimes listed as the last verse in the chronological order of revelation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage’s late revelation is cited to explain the relative scarcity of hadith on ribā’s detailed workings despite the later intricacy of its law.
rows.anchor: This fact is sometimes cited as a reason for the relative paucity of aḥādīth regarding the actual workings of ribā

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet’s Farewell Sermon at his final pilgrimage in AH 10, a little over two months before his death, also cancels and prohibits ribā.
rows.anchor: The cancellation and prohibition of ribā is also mentioned in the Prophet’s “Farewell Sermon” at the end of his last pilgrimage in AH 10

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The image of rising as if touched by Satan refers to usurers’ resurrection from their graves.
rows.anchor: Shall not rise except as one rises who is felled by the touch of Satan refers to how the usurers are resurrected out of their graves (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hadiths describe dire resurrection consequences for ribā offenders, including madness and choking or huge bellies with snakes emerging.
rows.anchor: Many aḥādīth speak of the terrible consequences on the Day of Judgment for those who are guilty of ribā

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says pre-Islamic ribā is forgiven but creditors retain principal, with neither side wronging the other; the added increase is canceled.
rows.anchor: a ḥadīth states, “Lo! All ribā from pre-Islamic times is forgiven. You shall have the principal of your wealth, and you shall neither wrong nor be wronged.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This rule concerns outstanding ribā only; past ribā cannot be reclaimed.
rows.anchor: This applied only to outstanding ribā; past ribā was not open to being reclaimed (Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the phrase about charity growing, “grow” is the verbal form of ribā; the commentary points to 2:261.
rows.anchor: In causes acts of charity to grow, grow is the verbal form of ribā. On the concept of causing charity to grow, see 2:261c.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alms are obligatory and integral to Muslim devotional and social life; institutional charity is contrasted with ribā as its moral opposite.
rows.anchor: Alms, mentioned here and in many other places, are obligatory and an integral dimension of Muslim devotional and social life.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet says that engaging in ribā ultimately brings loss even when it appears to produce growth.
rows.anchor: It is reported that the Prophet said, “The ultimate result for anyone who engages in ribā, even if that ribā brings growth, is loss.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse resembles the content of 2:62 and 5:69.
rows.anchor: This verse has content similar to that in 2:62 and 5:69.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternate rendering says that repentance leaves creditors their principal, neither wronging nor being wronged; accrued deferment increases are canceled while the original loan remains due.
rows.anchor: The second half of v. 279 can also be translated, “If you repent, you shall have the principal of your wealth, neither wronging nor being wronged.”

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the ribā participant will be challenged on Resurrection Day to take up a sword for war.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAbbās said, “On the Day of Resurrection it will be said to the one who partook of ribā, ‘Take up your sword for war!’”

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some interpret the war warning to mean ribā practitioners have made themselves enemies of or hostile to God and the Messenger.
rows.anchor: Some say that this means that they have made themselves the enemies of or hostile to God and the Messenger (Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ribā may justify legitimate authorities forcing violators to surrender their gains or fighting them if they refuse to desist.
rows.anchor: To practice ribā can be a cause for taking up arms against violators on the part of legitimate authority

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islamic loans, unlike investments, were ideally charitable because money’s time factor matters and credit sales or leases could serve non-charitable investment and fundraising.
rows.anchor: In the Islamic tradition, loans (as opposed to investments) were ideally charitable in nature, owing to the time factor in giving and taking money

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage invites creditors to turn ribā-laden loans into charity when debtors are in dire financial difficulty.
rows.anchor: in the case of a debtor in dire financial circumstances

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith credits a lender with one act of charity for each day of delay granted to someone in difficulty.
rows.anchor: A ḥadīth states, “Whosoever grants a delay to one in difficult circumstances shall be credited an act of charity for each day of it.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse encourages respite until the debtor has ease but does not require it or remove the lender’s claim to principal.
rows.anchor: This does not negate the claim of a lender to the original principal, since the verse encourages a respite until there is ease, but does not require it (Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ribā passage closes by reminding readers that all matters, including economic ones, will be accounted for in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: The passage on ribā ends with a reminder that all matters, including economic ones, will be accounted for in the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise that souls will not be wronged concerns ultimate destiny and echoes the phrase protecting the creditor’s principal in 2:279.
rows.anchor: It uses and they shall not be wronged in regard to a soul’s ultimate destiny, which is similar to the phrase used in connection with a creditor’s right to the loan principal in v. 279.

rows.speaker: Many
rows.claim: Many see the verse as an implicit argument against divinizing Christ because Jesus himself was once in the womb.
rows.anchor: Many see this verse as an implicit argument against divinizing Christ, as Jesus himself was once within the womb (IK, R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The development of the embryo in the womb is described more fully at 22:5.
rows.anchor: The development in the womb is described more fully in 22:5.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is often used as a prayer in Islamic piety.
rows.anchor: This verse is often used in Islamic piety as a prayer.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allāhumma addresses God in the second person; its etymology is disputed.
rows.anchor: O God translates Allāhumma, since this construction designates an address to God in the second person, but opinions differ over its etymology.

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some derive Allāhumma by shortening yā Allāhu ummanā bi-khayr, meaning “O God, bring us good.”
rows.anchor: Some consider it a shortening of yā Allāhu ummanā bi-khayr (“O God, bring us good”),

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others, judged less plausible by the author, say the suffix mīm replaces the usual vocative particle yā.
rows.anchor: but others suggest somewhat less plausibly that the mīm of the suffix takes the place of the traditional vocative particle yā

rows.speaker: some scholars
rows.claim: Some scholars speculate that Allāhumma comes from Aramaic or Akkadian.
rows.anchor: some scholars speculate that it comes from Aramaic or Akkadian.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allāhumma is unrelated to Elohim as a plural form.
rows.anchor: It is not related to the plural form, as is the case with the Hebrew Elohim.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mālik al-mulk is etymologically related internally and to malik, “king,” and malakūt, “dominion”; mulk can mean rule or possession.
rows.anchor: Master of Sovereignty renders mālik al-mulk, two words closely related etymologically to each other

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some recount that the Prophet asked for sovereignty over Byzantium and Persia for his religion, after which the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: Some recount that the Prophet asked for the sovereignty over Byzantium and Persia for his religion, after which this verse was revealed (Aj, R).

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some interpret mulk as prophethood, answering objections to Muhammad’s selection because he was not Israelite, prominent among Arabs, or an angel.
rows.anchor: Some say mulk here refers to prophethood (Ṭ) and could thus be meant to counter objections from various quarters to the selection of Muhammad as a prophet

rows.speaker: all commentators
rows.claim: All commentators understand “the good” to mean every possible good.
rows.anchor: All commentators understand the good to mean all possible good.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sawāʾ can mean just or fair and derives from a root associated with equality, straightness, soundness, proportion, or the middle; sawāʾ al-sabīl idiomatically means the right way.
rows.anchor: a word sometimes understood as meaning “just” or “fair.”

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some read the call as inviting the People of the Book to a just and fair word, rather than specifically to doctrines shared by Christianity, Judaism, and Islam.
rows.anchor: Thus this phrase is interpreted by some to mean not that the Quran is calling the People of the Book to observe what Christianity or Judaism have in common with Islam, but that this word (or these words) to which the Prophet is calling the People of the Book are just and fair (R).

rows.speaker: Al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī glosses the shared word as fair treatment by each side toward the other.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī glosses it thus: “Come to a word in which there is fair treatment from each of us to the other.”

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others accept “just” but explain it as common ground because each religion claims to worship God.
rows.anchor: Others, while accepting the gloss of “just,” go on to explain that it refers to what these religions have in common, since they all claim to worship God (M),

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others say sawāʾ means what the Quran, Torah, and Gospel do not differ about.
rows.anchor: and others similarly say that sawāʾ refers to that regarding which the Quran, the Torah, and the Gospel do not differ (Z).

rows.speaker: Ibn Masʿūd
rows.claim: Al-Thaʿlabī cites Ibn Masʿūd’s view that calling someone to a thing’s sawāʾ is calling them to its middle.
rows.anchor: Al-Thaʿlabī quotes an opinion of Ibn Masʿūd that to call some to the sawāʾ of something is to call them to the middle of it.

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some say the command addresses Jews in and around Madinah; others say it addresses Jews and Christians; some restrict it to Najrān’s Christians.
rows.anchor: For some, the command in this verse was meant to address the Jews in and around Madinah

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some explain taking one another as lords as prostrating before people; others mean obeying them against the truth.
rows.anchor: Some understand take one another as lords to mean that one prostrates before them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement about taking lords apart from God parallels 9:31’s account of rabbis, monks, and the Messiah being taken as lords despite the command to worship one God.
rows.anchor: This part of the verse is similar to 9:31: They have taken their rabbis and monks as lords apart from God

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: One report says Jews asked the Prophet whether he wanted to be worshipped as Jesus was among Christians.
rows.anchor: It is reported that the Prophet was asked by the Jews whether he wanted to be an object of worship, as Jesus was among the Christians (Ṭ),

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: Another report says he was asked whether people should prostrate to him instead of greeting him normally.
rows.anchor: or that he was asked whether he thought people should prostrate themselves before him (an act associated with worship) rather than greet him normally (Z).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥukm, translated as judgment, can also mean rule.
rows.anchor: Judgment (ḥukm) can also mean “rule.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿIbād, singular ʿabd, means worshippers of something.
rows.anchor: means to be worshippers of something.

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators connect the verse to Islam’s rejection of Jesus’ worship; it also condemns other worship of humans, as in 9:31.
rows.anchor: Although most commentators draw a connection between this verse and the Islamic rejection of the worship of Jesus, other types of worship directed at human beings are similarly deplored, as in 9:31

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse is thematically related to 5:116, where Jesus denies telling people to take him and his mother as gods apart from God.
rows.anchor: It is related thematically to 5:116: And when God said, “O Jesus son of Mary! Didst thou say unto mankind

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Rabbāniyyūn, translated “sages,” is variously understood as wise, knowledgeable, pious, or eminent religious scholars who know the lawful and forbidden.
rows.anchor: a word interpreted variously as meaning those who are wise, knowledgeable, or pious (Ṭ) or the most eminent of religious scholars who understand the lawful and the forbidden (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary directs readers to 5:43–44 for further discussion of rabbāniyyūn.
rows.anchor: on this term, see especially 5:43–44c.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The variant ribbiyyūn appears in 3:146 and is translated there as devoted men.
rows.anchor: A variant of rabbānī, ribbiyyūn, appears in 3:146

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: An alternate reading renders the final phrase as knowing the Book and teaching it.
rows.anchor: An alternate reading of the verse’s final phrase would give the translation, “from having known the Book and from having taught it” (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some read qātala as qutila, meaning the prophet was killed while many devoted men stood with him.
rows.anchor: And how many a prophet was killed, while there were alongside him many devoted men!

rows.speaker: Al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī prefers the “was killed” reading because it fits the plain sense of the preceding verses.
rows.anchor: Al-Ṭabarī prefers this interpretation, as it accords with the plain sense of the previous verses.

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some interpret ribbiyyūn as a form of rabbāniyyūn, translated as sages in 3:79.
rows.anchor: Devoted men translates ribbiyyūn, which is interpreted by some as a form of rabbāniyyūn, rendered in this translation as sages (Z; see v. 79).

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Others interpret ribbiyyūn generally as large groups; some specify ten thousand per ribbī and understand the word as many learned or patient people.
rows.anchor: Others suggest that it refers generally to large groups (Ṭ); some give ten thousand as the specific number for ribbī and interpret ribbiyyūn to mean large numbers of learned people (ʿulamāʾ; Ṭ) or patient people (Q).

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The covenant is understood as one made by prophets with their peoples by God’s Leave.
rows.anchor: God made the covenant is interpreted to mean that the prophets made a covenant with their peoples by God’s Leave (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the verse specifically concerns Jews, it can generally condemn anyone given knowledge who fails to teach it.
rows.anchor: This verse can be understood as a general condemnation of anyone who is given knowledge, but then does not teach it, even though it is speaking specifically of the Jews (Q).

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: The pronoun “it” refers to the Book, though some take it more specifically as prophecies of Muhammad’s coming in earlier scriptures.
rows.anchor: The it in make it clear . . . and not conceal it refers back to the Book, though some offer the interpretation that this refers more specifically to the foretellings of the coming of the Prophet Muhammad

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet warns that whoever conceals knowledge from their people will wear a bridle of Fire.
rows.anchor: The Prophet said, “Whosoever conceals knowledge from his people will wear one of the bridles of the Fire,”

rows.speaker: ʿAlī
rows.claim: ʿAlī says God requires learned people to teach before requiring ignorant people to learn.
rows.anchor: and ʿAlī said, “God tasks no ignorant person with learning until he tasks a learned person with teaching.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse belongs to a broader theme of the People of the Book concealing revelation, also found in the listed verses.
rows.anchor: On this theme of the People of the Book concealing what God has revealed to them, see also 2:42, 76, 140, 146, 159, 174; 3:71; 5:15; 6:91.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Casting the covenant and Book behind their backs means failing to commit to or live by their teachings.
rows.anchor: The casting aside of the covenant and the Book is also mentioned in 2:100–101 and refers to the lack of commitment to it and failure to live according to its teachings (R).
